content: Dexlansoprazole does not have any known interactions with food or drinks. However, it is unclear whether alcohol consumption affects the medication. Always inform your healthcare provider about all prescription and over-the-counter medications, vitamins, minerals, herbal products, and supplements you are taking. This is particularly important if you are using medications such as methotrexate, digoxin (used for irregular heartbeat and heart failure), warfarin (a blood thinner), tacrolimus (used to prevent organ transplant rejection), certain antiretroviral medications for HIV/AIDS (e.g., rilpivirine, nelfinavir, saquinavir), St. John’s Wort, or rifampin (used for tuberculosis). These medications may interact with dexlansoprazole, altering its blood levels or vice versa. Additionally, dexlansoprazole may affect the absorption of other medications. Always provide your healthcare provider with a complete list of medications you are currently or recently taking, as this list may not cover all potential interactions. If you or someone else accidentally takes too much dexlansoprazole, seek immediate medical attention, call 911, or contact a Poison Control Center at 800-222-1222. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and take only the next scheduled dose. Do not take double or extra doses. Dexlansoprazole is used to treat heartburn and conditions caused by excessive stomach acid, such as gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) and erosive esophagitis (EE). It may also be prescribed for other conditions as determined by your healthcare provider. The medication works by reducing the amount of acid produced in the stomach. Dexlansoprazole is available as Dexilant or generic dexlansoprazole in delayed-release oral capsules of 30 mg and 60 mg. The most common side effects of dexlansoprazole include diarrhea, stomach pain, nausea, cold symptoms, vomiting, gas, headache (in children aged 12 to 17), and sore throat (in children aged 12 to 17). If these side effects bother you, inform your healthcare provider. Other side effects not listed here may occur, so contact your healthcare provider if you suspect a side effect. Serious side effects, though less common, include kidney problems such as acute tubulointerstitial nephritis, which can occur at any time during treatment. Symptoms include decreased urine output or blood in the urine. Antibiotic-associated diarrhea caused by Clostridioides difficile (C. diff) overgrowth may also occur, with symptoms such as watery diarrhea, persistent diarrhea, blood in stool, severe stomach cramps, or fever. Severe skin reactions like Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) or Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN) can be life-threatening. Symptoms include painful red or purple skin that peels, flat red rashes or blisters on the skin, mouth, nose, or genitals, and red, painful, watery eyes. If you experience any of these symptoms, stop taking dexlansoprazole and seek immediate medical attention. Dexlansoprazole can also cause a severe allergic reaction called DRESS (Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms), which may affect multiple organs, including the liver, kidneys, and heart. Symptoms include skin rash, hives, fever, swollen lymph nodes, shortness of breath, swelling in the feet or legs, dark urine, or yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice). Stop the medication and seek immediate help if these symptoms occur. In rare cases, dexlansoprazole may trigger or worsen lupus, an autoimmune disorder. Symptoms include new or worsening joint pain or a rash on the arms or cheeks. Long-term use (three years or more) may lead to vitamin B-12 deficiency, with symptoms such as a sore tongue, weakness, or tingling in the hands or feet. It may also cause low magnesium levels (hypomagnesemia), which can result in seizures, heart rhythm problems, dizziness, muscle spasms, or changes in heart rate. Prolonged use or high doses may increase the risk of bone loss and fractures, particularly in older adults. Dexlansoprazole should not be used by individuals allergic to its ingredients, including other proton pump inhibitors. Inform your healthcare provider about all medications and supplements you are taking to avoid potential interactions. Do not take dexlansoprazole unless prescribed by a healthcare provider, and follow the prescribed instructions. Do not share this medication with others, even if they have similar symptoms, as it may harm them. Keep it out of reach of children. Dexlansoprazole capsules should not be chewed, cut, or crushed. They can be taken with or without food. If swallowing capsules is difficult, the contents can be sprinkled on one tablespoon of applesauce and swallowed immediately without mixing with other foods. If administered through a nasogastric (NG) tube, follow your healthcare provider’s instructions. This medication is not intended for immediate heartburn relief and may take one to four days to take full effect. Children under two years of age may be at greater risk for certain side effects. Discuss the risks with your healthcare provider if your child is under two years old. Before using dexlansoprazole, inform your healthcare provider about all health conditions, including low blood potassium, magnesium, calcium, or sodium levels, as well as liver problems. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, consult your healthcare provider, as it is unclear how dexlansoprazole may affect pregnancy or if it passes into breast milk.
